title: Is One a Rotation of the Other
statement:
A rotation moves some number of characters from the front of a string to its back, keeping their order. Rotating "canvas" by 2 gives "nvasca". Rotating by 0 leaves the string as it is.

Given strings s and goal, return true if some rotation of s equals goal, otherwise false.

examples.why: Move "but" from the front to the back.
Same letters, but a rotation never changes the cyclic order. Comparing letter counts is not enough.
"aba" sits inside "abab", but a rotation must keep the length.

constraints: s and goal contain lowercase English letters
hints: Try every possible rotation amount and compare. How many are there?
Write s twice in a row: s + s. What strings of length |s| appear inside it?
Every rotation of s is a window of length |s| inside s + s, and nothing else of that length is. So check lengths are equal and that goal occurs in s + s.

explain.intuition:
Glue s to itself. Reading s + s from position k for |s| characters gives exactly the rotation by k: the tail of the first copy followed by the head of the second. So the rotations of s are precisely the length-|s| windows of s + s.

That turns the question into a substring search, plus a length check. A built-in search is fine in an interview; if asked for a guaranteed linear time, use KMP or a rolling hash on s + s.
pitfalls: Skipping the length check. "aba" is inside "abab" but is not a rotation of "ab".
Comparing letter counts only. "abcd" and "acbd" have the same letters but different cyclic order.

complexity.time: O(n) with KMP (built-in search is usually fast in practice)

solutions.title: Try every shift
solutions.idea: For each rotation amount k, compare s rotated by k with goal character by character.

solutions.title: Search in the doubled string with KMP
solutions.idea: Every rotation of s is a window of s + s. Run KMP for goal over s + s so the search is linear even on inputs like "aaaa…ab".

followups: Return the smallest rotation amount that works, or −1.
Group a list of strings into classes that are rotations of each other. What key would you hash?
